title: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
gist: Publishers are beginning to treat AI agents, not humans, as the audience: Axios is launching Axios Direct, structured RSS-like feeds for agents (starting with M&A data for Axios Pro Deals subscribers, then LLM training and consumer feeds), while Every embeds prompts and agent-queryable reporting databases in its articles. Monetization remains immature; value is shifting to proprietary, market-moving or specialized information that LLMs lack.

insights.claim: Axios's CRO argues the open web is deteriorating, search is shrinking, hyperpersonalization is surging and LLMs are becoming central to news consumption, so a significant share of consumption will move into AI systems and devices.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Search-referral-dependent publishers and ad models face structural decline as consumption shifts to AI intermediaries.
insights.quote: We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging

insights.claim: Axios Direct delivers structured, low-narrative feeds designed for AI agents, which Axios likens more to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: News is being repackaged as machine-readable data products, converging with financial data terminals.

insights.claim: Axios is rolling out three Direct feeds: an M&A feed for Axios Pro Deals subscribers' agents launched this fall, an LLM-training feed next year, and a later consumer feed for individual subscribers' agents.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Content licensing for in-house LLM training is becoming a productized publisher revenue line.

insights.claim: Starting agent feeds with corporate clients makes sense because corporate budgets tolerate unproven experiments more than individual subscribers if they offer even a slight business edge.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: B2B is the likely first monetizable market for agent-oriented content.
insights.locator: Starting with feeds aimed at businesses

insights.claim: Every builds articles for AI-augmented readers by embedding copy-paste prompts, 'Read With Claude' / 'Read With ChatGPT' buttons, and reporting databases that let subscribers' agents generate tailored articles, podcasts or videos.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Content becomes a raw-material database rather than a fixed narrative, changing how editorial value is captured.
insights.locator: Certain types of articles—such as guides

insights.claim: Because agents extract the relevant bits, Every's writers pack stories with detail without worrying about losing human attention, and with AI journalists no longer have to choose what goes into a story for each reader.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Agent-mediated reading inverts the brevity incentive of attention-optimized media.

insights.claim: Publisher responses to AI split between licensing deals (such as Condé Nast's) plus generative engine optimization, and defensive litigation like The New York Times' ongoing 2023 copyright suit against OpenAI and Microsoft.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The outcome of the NYT case and the spread of licensing deals will set the price of training and retrieval content.
insights.locator: Major publishers have responded to that

insights.claim: Axios executives say its short-form, highly structured style already makes it a favorite source for AI crawlers answering prompts.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Format and structure, not just authority, determine which publishers win citations in AI answers.

insights.claim: Axios's COO frames AI not as the audience but as a distribution tool, comparable to earlier shifts to social media, short video and podcasts.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Suggests publishers may treat AI as a new channel rather than an existential threat, shaping their licensing stance.
insights.quote: It isn’t really AI as the audience

insights.claim: University of Copenhagen professor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen says the market for publishing to agents is emerging but immature and extremely uneven, with open questions on pricing and agent interaction.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: No established pricing model yet for agent consumption means revenue upside for publishers is speculative.

insights.claim: Nielsen argues AI surfacing a brand's content can carry visibility value even without site visits, much like publishers' content on TikTok and Instagram.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Zero-click AI distribution may be tolerated by publishers as brand marketing, weakening their negotiating leverage.

insights.claim: As chatbots commoditize answers, people will only pay for information other publications and LLMs lack, such as market-moving deal data or in-the-weeds AI guidance; Axios Pro Deals costs $2,499 a year versus $288 for Every.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Pricing power is concentrating in proprietary, time-sensitive and specialized information.
insights.quote: People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have.

insights.claim: Every's founder envisions subscriptions covering a human reader plus their agents, with the agent reading everything and flagging what matters.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Seat-based subscriptions may expand to agent licenses, creating new pricing tiers.
insights.quote: I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’

insights.claim: Every, a six-year-old tech media and software company, raised a $2 million round last year from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Small seed-scale bets are backing AI-native media formats.
